stem: A 20-year-old man is brought to the office for evaluation of abnormal behavior.  Over the past 4 months, the patient has had several episodes of unresponsiveness, during which he stared blankly while smacking his lips.  During each episode, he spontaneously became responsive after about 2 minutes and had no recollection of the event.  The patient says the episodes are often preceded by an uneasy sensation in his upper abdomen and the pungent smell of something burning.  He has had no falls or jerky movements of the extremities.  The patient has no history of recent fever, headaches, head trauma, nausea, vomiting, or focal neurologic deficits.  He had seizures in early childhood precipitated by high fever but has had none since.  He has no other medical conditions and takes no medications.  Cranial nerve examination reveals no abnormalities.  Motor strength, sensation, and deep tendon reflexes are normal throughout.  Neuroimaging is most likely to reveal an abnormality in which of the following locations in the brain?​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌
explanation:
In contrast to generalized seizures, which originate throughout the cerebral cortex, focal seizures originate in a single hemisphere.  They are subcategorized as follows:

  • Focal aware seizures:  Patients are aware and interactive but have symptoms corresponding to the involved area of the brain (eg, face or limb twitching/jerking - frontal lobe [motor cortex], auditory/olfactory auras - temporal lobe, visual hallucinations - occipital lobe).
  • Focal impaired awareness seizures:  Patients appear awake but do not interact appropriately (eg, blank stare) and frequently engage in repetitive, stereotyped automatisms (eg, lip smacking, hand wringing, repeating words).  These episodes can look like absence seizures, which are a type of generalized seizure; however, absence seizures usually occur in children and are much shorter (eg, <10 sec).

Focal seizures with impaired awareness are the typical manifestation of temporal lobe epilepsy.  Seizures are often preceded by a distinctive aura (eg, uneasy epigastric sensation, unpleasant olfactory hallucination) that helps localize the seizures to the mesial temporal lobe, the inner/medial aspect of the temporal lobe (eg, hippocampus, amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus).  The disorder is usually due to underlying hippocampal sclerosis, which is associated with childhood febrile seizures and can be seen on neuroimaging (eg, reduced hippocampal volume) or on postmortem histologic examination (eg, neuronal loss, chronic fibrillary gliosis).

(Choice A)  The cerebellar vermis is responsible for vestibular function, balance, and coordination.  Patients who have been taking phenytoin for several years can exhibit cerebellar atrophy with accompanying ataxia.  In contrast, this patient takes no medications and has no evidence of ataxia.

(Choice C)  The nondominant parietal lobe has a role in sensory integration and nonverbal spatial mapping and orientation.  A seizure affecting this part of the brain can cause paresthesia (eg, from postcentral gyrus) or distortions in a patient's sense of position (eg, a feeling of floating, changes in posture).

(Choice D)  The occipital pole contains the primary visual cortex.  Seizures that originate in the occipital pole characteristically have visual auras (eg, flashing lights, vision distortions, complex hallucinations).

(Choice E)  The premotor frontal cortex is responsible for the planning of motor movements.  A seizure affecting this part of the brain can result in abnormal posturing or repetitive movements, but abdominal and olfactory auras would not occur.

Educational objective:Recurrent focal impaired awareness seizures that are preceded by a distinctive aura (eg, uneasy epigastric sensation, olfactory hallucination) are characteristic of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.  The most common etiology is mesial temporal sclerosis, which is associated with childhood febrile seizures.​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌
